about: MATH0011 Mathematical Methods 2 is a 15-credit Term 2 module for first-year UCL Mathematics students, following on from MATH0010 Mathematical Methods 1. According to the 2026–27 syllabus it has two parts: about four weeks of programming for the mathematical sciences in Python, then about five weeks of multivariable calculus (coordinate systems, partial derivatives, curves, multiple integrals and vector fields up to Green's theorem and surface integrals). The 2026–27 assessment is a 75% examination, a 20% programming project and 5% vector calculus written coursework; you need at least 40% in the exam and 40% overall to pass.
topics: Python basics: running code, variables, loops and conditionals
Types and data structures: numbers, strings, lists, tuples and dictionaries
Debugging, plotting, matrices and numerical calculus in Python
Partial derivatives, gradient, directional derivatives and the chain rule
Taylor series and critical points of functions of two variables
Double and triple integrals, Jacobians and change of variables
Vector fields: line integrals, divergence, curl and potentials

notes.h: Python basics: running code, variables, loops and conditionals
notes.body:
The first part of MATH0011 (about four weeks in the 2026–27 syllabus) teaches programming in Python, with the emphasis on writing correct programs that solve mathematical problems. This note covers the building blocks you will use in every later program.

Running code, input and output
- A program is a text file (for example primes.py) run by the Python interpreter, or code typed into an interactive session or notebook cell.
- print(...) writes to the screen. input("Prompt: ") reads what the user types, always as a string, so convert it: n = int(input("n = ")).

Variables and arithmetic
- A variable is a name bound to a value: x = 3. Assignment uses a single =; comparison uses ==.
- a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line.
- Operators: + − * as usual; / is true division and always gives a float (7/2 is 3.5); // is floor division, which rounds down towards minus infinity (7//2 is 3 but −7//2 is −4); % is the remainder, which takes the sign of the divisor (−7 % 3 is 2), so that a == (a//b)*b + a%b always holds; ** is a power (2**10 is 1024).
- Two traps: ^ is not a power (2^3 is the bitwise operation XOR and gives 1), and ** binds more tightly than a leading minus, so −2**2 is −4.

Conditionals
- if / elif / else run different blocks depending on Boolean tests built from ==, !=, <, <=, and, or, not.
- Indentation (normally four spaces) defines the block. A missing colon or inconsistent indentation is a syntax error.

Loops
- for n in range(a, b): runs n = a, a+1, …, b−1 (the end point is excluded). range(0, 10, 3) gives 0, 3, 6, 9.
- while condition: repeats as long as the condition is True. Make sure something in the body changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
- break leaves the loop at once; continue skips the rest of the current pass and goes to the next one.

Worked example: sum of squares
- s = 0, then for n in range(1, 6): s += n**2, then print(s). Output: 55, since 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 55.

Worked example: first triangular number above 1000
- n = 0 and s = 0; while s <= 1000: n += 1 and s += n. The loop stops at n = 45 with s = 1035 (n = 44 gives only 990). This matches solving n(n+1)/2 > 1000.

Good habits
- Test your loop on a small case you can check by hand before trusting it on a big one.
- Use meaningful names (total, count) and comments for anything non-obvious.
- Watch off-by-one errors at the ends of ranges.

Exam tips: when asked "what does this code print?", trace it line by line in a small table of variable values. Pay special attention to range end points, // and % with negative numbers, and whether a continue or break is reached first.

Every value in Python has a type, and many bugs come from using the wrong one. The 2026–27 syllabus lists strings, integers and floats, then lists, tuples and dictionaries.

Numbers
- int: whole numbers of unlimited size (2**100 is exact).
- float: double-precision floating point, about 15–17 significant decimal digits. Most decimals cannot be stored exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004 and 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False.
- Compare floats with a tolerance: abs(a − b) < 1e-12, or math.isclose(a, b).
- Conversions: int("7") is 7; float("2.5") is 2.5; str(3) is "3". int(3.9) is 3 and int(−3.9) is −3 (it truncates towards zero). round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4, because Python rounds exact halves to the even neighbour.
- complex numbers are built in: 1 + 2j.
- bool has the values True and False.

Strings
- Text in quotes: "maths". Strings are sequences, so s[0] is the first character and len(s) is the length.
- + joins strings ("7" + "3" is "73", not 10) and * repeats them ("ab" * 3 is "ababab").
- Strings are immutable: s[0] = "H" raises a TypeError. Build a new string instead.
- f-strings format numbers: f"{x:.3f}" shows x to 3 decimal places.

Lists
- Ordered, mutable collections: L = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]. Indices start at 0, and L[-1] is the last item (50).
- Slicing L[a:b] includes index a but not b: L[1:3] is [20, 30]; L[::2] is [10, 30, 50].
- Methods: append, insert, pop, sort; len(L) gives the length.
- Assignment does not copy. After b = a, both names refer to the same list, so b.append(4) changes a as well. Use b = a.copy() or b = a[:] for a (shallow) copy.
- List comprehensions build lists compactly: [n**2 for n in range(5)] is [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].

Tuples
- Ordered and immutable: t = (1, 2, 3). t[0] = 5 raises a TypeError.
- Useful for fixed records such as coordinates, and for returning several values from a function.

Dictionaries
- Map keys to values: d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}; d["c"] = 3 adds an entry.
- Keys must be hashable, which in practice means immutable: strings, numbers and tuples are fine; lists, sets and dictionaries are not.
- d["z"] raises a KeyError if "z" is missing; d.get("z", 0) returns a default instead. "a" in d tests for a key.
- Since Python 3.7, dictionaries remember insertion order.

Worked example: counting
- counts = {}; for w in words: counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1. This counts how often each word appears without needing to check whether the key exists first.

Exam tips: be ready to predict the result of slicing, aliasing (b = a) and float comparisons, and to say which types are mutable (list, dict) and which are not (int, float, str, tuple).

Functions, classes and modules let you organise code into reusable, testable pieces. The 2026–27 syllabus lists functions with local and global variables, classes, instances and objects, and creating and importing modules.

Functions
- def name(parameters): followed by an indented body. return sends a value back; a function with no return statement returns None.
- Default and keyword arguments: def trap(f, a, b, n=100) can be called as trap(g, 0, 1) or trap(g, 0, 1, n=1000).
- Functions are objects, so you can pass one as an argument. A numerical integrator that takes the integrand f as a parameter is the standard example; lambda x: x**2 creates a small unnamed function.
- Trap: default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. With def f(x, L=[]): L.append(x); return L, the calls f(1) and then f(2) return [1] and then [1, 2], because the same list is reused. Use L=None and create a new list inside the function.

Scope: local and global variables
- A name assigned inside a function is local to that function. With x = 5 outside and def h(): x = 10; return x, calling h() gives 10 but leaves the global x equal to 5.
- If a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, that name is local throughout the function, so reading it before the assignment raises an UnboundLocalError.
- The global keyword lets a function rebind a global name, but passing values in as arguments and returning results is clearer and easier to test.
- Python looks names up in the order Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in (the LEGB rule).

Classes, instances and objects
- A class defines a new type; an instance (object) is one value of that type.
- __init__ sets up a new instance's attributes; self is the instance itself and is the first parameter of every method.
- Example: class Vector2 with __init__(self, x, y) storing self.x and self.y, a method norm(self) returning (self.x**2 + self.y**2)**0.5, and __add__(self, other) returning Vector2(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y). Then Vector2(3, 4).norm() is 5.0, and v + w works because of __add__.
- Special methods such as __add__, __mul__ and __repr__ let your objects use operators and print nicely.

Modules
- Any .py file is a module. import math then math.sqrt(2); from math import sqrt then sqrt(2); import numpy as np for an abbreviated name.
- Code under if __name__ == "__main__": runs only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported. Put tests and demonstrations there.

Exam tips: be able to trace code involving local versus global names and mutable default arguments, and to write a short class with __init__ and one or two methods. State what a function returns when it has no return statement (None).

notes.h: Debugging, plotting, matrices and numerical calculus
notes.body:
The last weeks of the programming part (2026–27 syllabus) cover debugging and error handling, plotting, matrices and vectors, and numerical differentiation and integration. In Python these are usually done with the NumPy and Matplotlib libraries.

Errors and debugging
- SyntaxError: the code cannot be parsed (missing colon, bracket or indentation). NameError: a name is used before it is defined. TypeError: an operation on the wrong type, e.g. "a" + 1. ValueError: right type, bad value, e.g. int("abc"). IndexError: list index out of range. KeyError: missing dictionary key. ZeroDivisionError: 1/0.
- Read a traceback from the bottom: the last line names the error and the lines above show where it happened.
- try: … except ValueError: … handles an expected error; raise signals one; assert checks a condition you believe must hold.
- Strategies: test on cases with known answers, print intermediate values, change one thing at a time, and use a debugger to step through.

Plotting and arrays
- x = np.linspace(0, 1, 5) gives the five equally spaced points 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.
- import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; plt.plot(x, y); add axis labels, a title and a legend; plt.show() or plt.savefig(...).
- For A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) and B = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]): A * B is elementwise, [[0, 2], [3, 0]]; A @ B is the matrix product, [[2, 1], [4, 3]].
- np.linalg.solve(A, b) solves Ax = b; for b = (5, 6) it gives x = (−4, 4.5).

Numerical differentiation
- Forward difference: f′(x) ≈ (f(x+h) − f(x))/h, error proportional to h (first order), by Taylor's theorem.
- Central difference: f′(x) ≈ (f(x+h) − f(x−h))/(2h), error proportional to h² (second order), because the h² terms of the two Taylor expansions cancel.
- Example, f = eˣ at x = 0 (true value 1), h = 0.1: forward gives 1.05171 (error about 0.052), central gives 1.00167 (error about 0.0017).
- Round-off: making h very small causes cancellation in f(x+h) − f(x). For the forward difference of eˣ at x = 1, the error is about 7 × 10⁻⁹ at h = 10⁻⁸ but about 4 × 10⁻⁴ at h = 10⁻¹².

Numerical integration (n equal steps of width h)
- Trapezium rule: h[½f₀ + f₁ + … + fₙ₋₁ + ½fₙ]. Error proportional to h² (for f with a continuous second derivative): halving h roughly quarters the error.
- Simpson's rule (n even): (h/3)[f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + 4f₃ + … + 4fₙ₋₁ + fₙ]. Error proportional to h⁴, and exact for cubics.
- Example: ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3 with n = 4: trapezium gives 0.34375, Simpson gives 0.33333… exactly.
- Example: ∫₀¹ eˣ dx: trapezium errors are 0.00894 (n = 4) and 0.00224 (n = 8), a ratio of about 4; Simpson errors fall by a factor of about 16.

Exam tips: be able to derive the error order of a difference formula from Taylor series, apply the trapezium and Simpson rules by hand to a few points, and say what happens to the error when h is halved.

The multivariable calculus part of MATH0011 begins with coordinate systems, because many integrals and fields are far simpler in coordinates that match the symmetry of the problem.

Polar coordinates in 2D
- x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, with r ≥ 0. Conversely r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x.
- tan θ = y/x does not fix the quadrant. For (−1, 1), arctan(y/x) gives −π/4, but the point is in the second quadrant, so θ = 3π/4 (with r = √2). In code use math.atan2(y, x), which handles the quadrant.
- θ is defined only up to multiples of 2π, and is undefined at the origin.
- Curves: r = a is a circle; θ = α is a half-line from the origin. r = 2 cos θ gives r² = 2r cos θ, i.e. x² + y² = 2x, the circle (x − 1)² + y² = 1.
- Area element: dA = r dr dθ, because a small polar "rectangle" has sides dr and r dθ.
- Unit vectors: e_r = (cos θ, sin θ) and e_θ = (−sin θ, cos θ). These change with position, which is why the velocity of a moving point is ṙ e_r + r θ̇ e_θ.

Cylindrical polar coordinates in 3D
- Polar coordinates in the xy-plane plus height: x = ρ cos φ, y = ρ sin φ, z = z (some texts write r, θ, z).
- Volume element: dV = ρ dρ dφ dz.
- Example: (√3, 1, 5) has ρ = 2, φ = π/6, z = 5.
- Natural for cylinders, pipes and anything with an axis of symmetry.

Spherical polar coordinates in 3D
- In the convention used here: r ≥ 0 is the distance from the origin, θ ∈ [0, π] is the angle from the positive z-axis, and φ ∈ [0, 2π) is the azimuthal angle around the z-axis.
- x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ.
- Volume element: dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ. The three edges of a small box are dr, r dθ and r sin θ dφ.
- Surfaces: r = constant is a sphere; θ = constant is a cone; φ = constant is a half-plane.
- Example: (r, θ, φ) = (2, π/3, π/4) gives x = y = 2(√3/2)(√2/2) = √6/2 ≈ 1.225 and z = 2 cos(π/3) = 1. Conversely (1, 1, √2) has r = 2, θ = arccos(√2/2) = π/4 and φ = π/4.
- Warning: conventions differ between books (some swap θ and φ, and geography measures latitude from the equator). Always state which you are using, and use the one your lecture notes use in the exam.

Exam tips: always sketch the region and decide which coordinate system matches it. Check the quadrant when finding θ or φ, and never forget the Jacobian factor (r, ρ or r² sin θ) when you change variables in an integral.

notes.h: Partial derivatives, gradient, directional derivatives and the chain rule
notes.body:
For a function f(x, y) of two variables, partial derivatives measure the rate of change in one coordinate direction with the other held fixed.

Partial derivatives
- f_x(a, b) = lim (f(a + h, b) − f(a, b))/h as h → 0, and similarly for f_y.
- Example: f = x²y + sin(xy) gives f_x = 2xy + y cos(xy) and f_y = x² + x cos(xy).
- Second derivatives: f_xx, f_yy and the mixed derivatives f_xy, f_yx.
- Symmetry of mixed partials (Schwarz/Clairaut): if f_xy and f_yx both exist and are continuous on an open set containing (a, b), then f_xy(a, b) = f_yx(a, b).

Linear approximation and tangent planes
- f is differentiable at (a, b) if f(a + h, b + k) = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)h + f_y(a, b)k + E, where E/√(h² + k²) → 0 as (h, k) → (0, 0).
- Sufficient condition: if f_x and f_y exist near (a, b) and are continuous at (a, b), then f is differentiable there.
- Partial derivatives existing is not enough. f = xy/(x² + y²) with f(0, 0) = 0 has f_x(0, 0) = f_y(0, 0) = 0 (f is zero on both axes), yet along y = x it equals ½, so it is not even continuous at the origin.
- Tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at (a, b): z = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x − a) + f_y(a, b)(y − b).
- Example: f = √(x² + y²) at (3, 4) has f = 5, f_x = 3/5, f_y = 4/5. So f(3.02, 3.97) ≈ 5 + 0.6(0.02) + 0.8(−0.03) = 4.988 (true value 4.98812).

Gradient and directional derivatives
- ∇f = (f_x, f_y) (or (f_x, f_y, f_z) in 3D).
- For differentiable f and a unit vector u, the rate of change in direction u is D_u f = ∇f · u.
- Since ∇f · u = |∇f| cos α, the maximum rate of increase is |∇f|, in the direction of ∇f; the rate is zero along level curves, so ∇f is perpendicular to level curves (and to level surfaces in 3D).
- Example: f = x² + 3xy at (1, 2): ∇f = (2x + 3y, 3x) = (8, 3). In the direction of (3, 4), u = (3/5, 4/5) and D_u f = (24 + 12)/5 = 7.2. The maximum rate is √73 ≈ 8.544.

Chain rule
- If x(t), y(t) are differentiable and f is differentiable at (x(t), y(t)), then z = f(x(t), y(t)) has dz/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt.
- If x = x(s, t) and y = y(s, t), then ∂z/∂s = f_x x_s + f_y y_s, and similarly for t.
- Example: z = x²y with x = cos t, y = sin t: dz/dt = 2xy(−sin t) + x² cos t. At t = π/4 this is −√2/2 + √2/4 = −√2/4 ≈ −0.354.
- Polar example: with x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, ∂z/∂θ = −r sin θ f_x + r cos θ f_y = −y f_x + x f_y.

Exam tips: always normalise the direction vector before using ∇f · u, state the hypotheses (continuity, differentiability) when quoting theorems, and draw a tree diagram for chain-rule problems with several layers of variables.

Taylor's theorem in two variables lets you approximate f near a point by a polynomial, and the quadratic terms decide what kind of critical point you have.

Second-order Taylor polynomial
- About (a, b), with h = x − a and k = y − b and all derivatives evaluated at (a, b):
  f(a + h, b + k) ≈ f + h f_x + k f_y + ½(h² f_xx + 2hk f_xy + k² f_yy).
- If f has continuous second partial derivatives near (a, b), the error is small compared with h² + k² as (h, k) → (0, 0).
- Example 1: eˣ cos y about (0, 0): f = 1, f_x = 1, f_y = 0, f_xx = 1, f_xy = 0, f_yy = −1, so P₂ = 1 + x + ½x² − ½y². At (0.1, 0.2), P₂ = 1.085 while the true value is 1.0831.
- Example 2: x²y about (1, 2): f = 2, f_x = 2xy = 4, f_y = x² = 1, f_xx = 2y = 4, f_xy = 2x = 2, f_yy = 0, so P₂ = 2 + 4h + k + 2h² + 2hk. At (1.1, 2.05), P₂ = 2.48 against the true 2.4805.

Critical points
- (a, b) is a critical (stationary) point if ∇f(a, b) = 0. At such a point the linear terms vanish, so the shape is set by the quadratic part, through the Hessian matrix H = [[f_xx, f_xy], [f_xy, f_yy]].
- Second derivative test. Suppose f has continuous second partial derivatives on a disc around (a, b) and ∇f(a, b) = 0. Let D = f_xx f_yy − f_xy² at (a, b).
  - D > 0 and f_xx > 0: local minimum.
  - D > 0 and f_xx < 0: local maximum.
  - D < 0: saddle point.
  - D = 0: the test is inconclusive.
- Equivalently: both eigenvalues of H positive gives a minimum, both negative a maximum, and opposite signs a saddle.

Worked example 1: f = x³ − 3x + y² − 2y
- f_x = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1; f_y = 2y − 2 = 0 gives y = 1.
- f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 2, f_xy = 0.
- At (1, 1): D = 12 > 0 with f_xx = 6 > 0, a local minimum with value −3.
- At (−1, 1): D = −12 < 0, a saddle point (f = 1).

Worked example 2: f = x³ + y³ − 3xy
- f_x = 3x² − 3y and f_y = 3y² − 3x. Setting both to zero gives y = x² and x = y², so x⁴ = x and the critical points are (0, 0) and (1, 1).
- D = (6x)(6y) − 9 = 36xy − 9. At (0, 0), D = −9: saddle. At (1, 1), D = 27 > 0 and f_xx = 6 > 0: local minimum, value −1.

When D = 0
- x⁴ + y⁴ (minimum), −x⁴ − y⁴ (maximum) and x⁴ − y⁴ (saddle) all have D = 0 at the origin, so you must look at the function directly.

Local versus global
- The test is local. On a closed, bounded region a continuous f attains a global maximum and minimum, which may lie on the boundary, so check the boundary separately.

Exam tips: find all critical points by solving ∇f = 0 systematically (no lost cases from dividing by zero), tabulate f_xx, f_yy, f_xy and D at each, and quote the test's hypothesis (continuous second partials).

A vector function r(t) = (x(t), y(t), z(t)) traces a curve as t varies, like the path of a particle with t as time.

Velocity, speed and acceleration
- Velocity (tangent vector): r′(t) = (x′(t), y′(t), z′(t)).
- Speed: |r′(t)|. Acceleration: r″(t).
- The curve is smooth where r′ is continuous and non-zero. The unit tangent is T = r′/|r′|.
- Differentiation rules: (u · v)′ = u′ · v + u · v′ and (u × v)′ = u′ × v + u × v′. If |r(t)| is constant, then r · r′ = 0, so the velocity is perpendicular to the position vector (as in circular motion).

Arc length
- The length of the curve for a ≤ t ≤ b is L = ∫ₐᵇ |r′(t)| dt.
- For a one-to-one parametrisation that traces the curve once, the length does not depend on which parametrisation you use.
- For a graph y = f(x): L = ∫ √(1 + f′(x)²) dx.
- The arc length function s(t) = ∫ₐᵗ |r′(u)| du satisfies ds/dt = |r′(t)|.

Worked examples
- Helix r = (cos t, sin t, t): r′ = (−sin t, cos t, 1), speed √2, so one turn (0 ≤ t ≤ 2π) has length 2√2 π ≈ 8.886.
- Helix r = (3 cos t, 3 sin t, 4t): speed √(9 + 16) = 5, so one turn has length 10π.
- y = x^(3/2) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4: f′ = (3/2)x^(1/2), so L = ∫₀⁴ √(1 + 9x/4) dx = (8/27)[(1 + 9x/4)^(3/2)]₀⁴ = (8/27)(10√10 − 1) ≈ 9.073.
- Cycloid r = (t − sin t, 1 − cos t), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π: speed = √(2 − 2 cos t) = 2 sin(t/2), so L = ∫₀^(2π) 2 sin(t/2) dt = 8.
- r = (t, t², 2t³/3): |r′|² = 1 + 4t² + 4t⁴ = (1 + 2t²)², so the length from 0 to 1 is ∫₀¹ (1 + 2t²) dt = 5/3. Spotting a perfect square like this is a common exam trick.

Integration with respect to arc length
- For a scalar function f, ∫_C f ds = ∫ₐᵇ f(r(t)) |r′(t)| dt. It gives, for example, the mass of a wire with density f.
- This integral does not depend on the direction in which C is traversed (ds is always positive). By contrast, the line integral of a vector field, ∫ F · dr, changes sign when the direction is reversed.
- Example: along one turn of the helix (cos t, sin t, t), ∫ (x² + y² + z) ds = ∫₀^(2π) (1 + t)√2 dt = √2(2π + 2π²) ≈ 36.80.

Exam tips: simplify |r′(t)| before integrating (look for perfect squares or trigonometric identities such as 1 − cos t = 2 sin²(t/2)), and keep track of whether an integral is with respect to t, s or a vector line element.

notes.h: Double and triple integrals, Jacobians and change of variables
notes.body:
Multiple integrals add up a quantity over an area or a volume. In practice you evaluate them as iterated single integrals, choosing the order and the coordinates to make the work easy.

Double integrals and Fubini's theorem
- ∬_R f dA is defined as a limit of Riemann sums over small rectangles.
- Fubini's theorem: if f is continuous on the rectangle R = [a, b] × [c, d], then ∬_R f dA = ∫ₐᵇ (∫_c^d f dy) dx = ∫_c^d (∫ₐᵇ f dx) dy.
- Example: ∬ xy dA over [0, 1] × [0, 2] = (∫₀¹ x dx)(∫₀² y dy) = ½ × 2 = 1.

General regions
- Type I: a ≤ x ≤ b, g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x); integrate in y first. Type II: c ≤ y ≤ d, h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y); integrate in x first.
- Example: R is under y = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Then ∬_R x dA = ∫₀¹ ∫₀^(x²) x dy dx = ∫₀¹ x³ dx = ¼.
- Reversing the order: ∫₀¹ ∫_y¹ e^(x²) dx dy cannot be done as written, since e^(x²) has no elementary antiderivative. The region is the triangle 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1, so the integral equals ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ e^(x²) dy dx = ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx = (e − 1)/2 ≈ 0.859. Always sketch the region before swapping.

Change of variables
- Theorem: let T(u, v) = (x(u, v), y(u, v)) have continuous first partial derivatives and map a region S one-to-one (except possibly on its boundary) onto R, with Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = x_u y_v − x_v y_u non-zero on the interior of S. If f is continuous on R, then ∬_R f dx dy = ∬_S f(x(u, v), y(u, v)) |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| du dv.
- Note the absolute value of the Jacobian.
- Polar: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ has Jacobian r, so dA = r dr dθ.
- Example: ∬ over the disc x² + y² ≤ a² of e^(−(x² + y²)) dA = ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀ᵃ e^(−r²) r dr dθ = π(1 − e^(−a²)). Letting a → ∞ gives π, which is the classic route to ∫ e^(−x²) dx = √π over the whole real line.
- Example: R is the square |x| + |y| ≤ 1. Put u = x + y, v = x − y, so x = (u + v)/2 and y = (u − v)/2. The Jacobian is −½, absolute value ½, and R becomes −1 ≤ u, v ≤ 1. So ∬_R (x + y)² dA = ½ ∫∫ u² du dv = ½ × (2/3) × 2 = 2/3.
- Example: the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² ≤ 1 becomes the unit disc under x = au, y = bv (Jacobian ab), so its area is πab.

Triple integrals
- ∭_V f dV, evaluated as three iterated integrals.
- Cylindrical: dV = ρ dρ dφ dz. Example: the volume between z = x² + y² and z = 4 is ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀² (4 − ρ²) ρ dρ dφ = 8π.
- Spherical: dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ. Example: the ball of radius a has volume ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀^π ∫₀ᵃ r² sin θ dr dθ dφ = 4πa³/3.

Exam tips: sketch the region, write the limits with the inner variables depending only on the outer ones, include the Jacobian (with absolute value), and check the result with a special case such as f = 1, which should give the area or volume.

notes.h: Vector fields: line integrals, divergence, curl and potentials
notes.body:
A vector field assigns a vector F(x, y, z) = (P, Q, R) to each point, for example a force field or a fluid velocity.

Line integrals of vector fields
- For a curve C parametrised by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b: ∫_C F · dr = ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t)) · r′(t) dt. Also written ∫_C P dx + Q dy + R dz.
- For a force F this is the work done along C. Reversing the direction of C changes the sign.
- Example: F = (y, −x) around the unit circle anticlockwise, r = (cos t, sin t): F · r′ = −sin²t − cos²t = −1, so the integral is −2π.

Divergence and curl
- div F = ∇ · F = P_x + Q_y + R_z, a scalar: the net outflow per unit volume (a source or sink).
- curl F = ∇ × F = (R_y − Q_z, P_z − R_x, Q_x − P_y), a vector: the local rotation.
- Example: F = (x², yz, xz) has div F = 2x + z + x = 3x + z and curl F = (0 − y, 0 − z, 0 − 0) = (−y, −z, 0). At (1, 2, 3): div F = 6 and curl F = (−2, −3, 0).
- Identities, for fields with continuous second partial derivatives: curl(∇φ) = 0 and div(curl F) = 0.

Conservative fields and potentials
- F is conservative if F = ∇φ for some scalar potential φ. (Physics often writes F = −∇V; that only changes the sign.)
- Fundamental theorem for line integrals: if C is a piecewise smooth curve from A to B and ∇φ is continuous on C, then ∫_C ∇φ · dr = φ(B) − φ(A).
- So for a continuous F on an open connected region, these are equivalent: F is conservative; ∫_C F · dr depends only on the end points (path independence); ∮ F · dr = 0 around every closed curve.
- Test in 2D: if P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives on an open simply connected region, then F = (P, Q) is conservative there if and only if P_y = Q_x. In 3D the test is curl F = 0 on a simply connected region.

Finding a potential
- F = (2xy, x² + 3y²): P_y = 2x = Q_x, so F is conservative on the whole plane.
- Integrate P with respect to x: φ = x²y + g(y). Then φ_y = x² + g′(y) = x² + 3y², so g = y³ and φ = x²y + y³.
- So ∫ F · dr from (0, 0) to (1, 2) is φ(1, 2) − φ(0, 0) = 2 + 8 = 10 along any path.

When the test fails
- F = (y, x²) has P_y = 1 and Q_x = 2x, so it is not conservative. From (0, 0) to (1, 1): along y = x the integral is ∫₀¹ (t + t²) dt = 5/6; along y = x³ it is ∫₀¹ (t³ + 3t⁴) dt = 17/20.
- Why simple connectivity matters: F = (−y, x)/(x² + y²) satisfies Q_x = P_y everywhere except the origin, yet its integral round the unit circle is 2π, not 0. The plane with the origin removed has a hole, so the test does not apply.

Exam tips: check conservativeness before parametrising (it can save a lot of work), always state the domain when you use the curl test, and keep the order of components in the curl formula straight.

Green's theorem links a line integral round a closed curve to a double integral over the region inside it. Surface integrals extend integration to curved surfaces in 3D.

Green's theorem
- Statement: let C be a positively oriented (anticlockwise, region on the left), piecewise smooth, simple closed curve bounding a region D, and let P and Q have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing D. Then ∮_C P dx + Q dy = ∬_D (Q_x − P_y) dA.
- Q_x − P_y is the k-component of curl(P, Q, 0), so Green's theorem says the circulation round C is the total "rotation" inside.

Examples
- Unit square [0, 1]², P = x² − y, Q = x + y²: Q_x − P_y = 1 − (−1) = 2, so the anticlockwise integral is 2 × area = 2. Working out all four sides directly gives the same answer.
- Unit circle, ∮ −y³ dx + x³ dy: Q_x − P_y = 3x² + 3y², so the integral is ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀¹ 3r³ dr dθ = 3π/2.
- Triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), ∮ xy dx + x² dy: Q_x − P_y = 2x − x = x, and ∬ x dA = 1/6.

Area from a line integral
- Choosing Q_x − P_y = 1 gives Area(D) = ∮ x dy = −∮ y dx = ½ ∮ (x dy − y dx).
- Ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t: ½ ∫₀^(2π) (ab cos²t + ab sin²t) dt = πab.

When the hypotheses fail
- For F = (−y, x)/(x² + y²) round the unit circle, Q_x − P_y = 0 wherever it is defined, yet the line integral is 2π. There is no contradiction, because P and Q are not differentiable (not even defined) at the origin, which lies inside C.
- For regions with holes, the boundary includes the inner curves traversed clockwise, so the region is always on the left.

Surface integrals
- A surface S is parametrised by r(u, v) for (u, v) in a region D. The vector r_u × r_v is normal to S, and the surface element is dS = |r_u × r_v| du dv.
- Scalar surface integral: ∬_S f dS = ∬_D f(r(u, v)) |r_u × r_v| du dv (with f = 1 this gives the area).
- Flux of a vector field: ∬_S F · dS = ∬_D F(r(u, v)) · (r_u × r_v) du dv, provided r_u × r_v points in the chosen direction (otherwise change the sign).
- Sphere of radius a: r = (a sin θ cos φ, a sin θ sin φ, a cos θ) gives r_θ × r_φ = a² sin θ (sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, cos θ), outward, with |r_θ × r_φ| = a² sin θ. Area = 4πa².
- Graph z = g(x, y): dS = √(1 + g_x² + g_y²) dx dy, and the upward flux is ∬ (−P g_x − Q g_y + R) dx dy.

Examples
- Flux of F = (x, y, z) outward through the sphere of radius a: on the sphere F · n = a, so the flux is a × 4πa² = 4πa³.
- Flux of (0, 0, z) up through the upper hemisphere of radius a: ∫∫ a³ cos²θ sin θ dθ dφ = 2πa³/3.
- Area of the paraboloid z = x² + y² over x² + y² ≤ 1: ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀¹ √(1 + 4r²) r dr dθ = (π/6)(5√5 − 1) ≈ 5.33.

Exam tips: check orientation (anticlockwise for Green's theorem; the direction of the normal for flux), state the hypotheses, and look for symmetry (such as F · n being constant on a sphere) before grinding through a parametrisation.

questions.q: In Python, what are the values of −7 // 2 and −7 % 2?
questions.why: Floor division rounds down, so −7 // 2 = −4, and the remainder must satisfy −7 = (−4)(2) + r, giving r = 1. The pair −3 and −1 comes from rounding towards zero, as some other languages do. −3.5 is the result of true division /, not //. The pair −4 and −1 gets the quotient right but gives the remainder the sign of the dividend, and (−4)(2) − 1 = −9, not −7.

questions.q: Write a short Python program using a while loop that finds the smallest positive integer n for which 1 + 2 + … + n > 1000, and state the value it prints. Explain why your loop terminates.
markScheme: Initialises a counter and running total (e.g. n = 0, s = 0)
Correct while condition (s <= 1000) with n incremented and added to s inside the loop
Prints n and states the answer n = 45 (s = 1035; n = 44 gives 990)
Explains termination: s strictly increases each pass so it must eventually exceed 1000
questions.modelAnswer:
n = 0
s = 0
while s <= 1000:
    n += 1
    s += n
print(n)

This prints 45: the sum to 44 is 990, which is not above 1000, and the sum to 45 is 1035. The loop terminates because s increases by at least 1 on every pass, so after finitely many passes s > 1000 and the condition becomes False.

questions.q:
What does this code print?

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)
questions.why: b = a makes b a second name for the same list, so appending through b changes the list that a refers to, and [1, 2, 3, 4] is printed. [1, 2, 3] assumes assignment makes a copy, which it does not. [4, 1, 2, 3] assumes append adds the new item at the front, but append always adds to the end (insert(0, 4) would put it at the front). None is what append itself returns, which you would see from print(b.append(4)), but here we print a.

questions.q: Which of the following can be used as a key in a Python dictionary?
questions.why: Dictionary keys must be hashable, and the tuple (1, 2) is immutable and hashable, so it works. The list [1, 2] is mutable and raises 'unhashable type: list'. The set {1, 2} is also mutable and unhashable (a frozenset would work). The dictionary {1: 2} is mutable too, so it cannot be a key.

questions.q: Explain why the Python expression 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to False, and describe how you would correctly test whether two floats are equal in a numerical program.
markScheme: Floats are stored in binary with finite precision (double precision, about 16 significant digits)
0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 cannot be represented exactly, so the computed sum is 0.30000000000000004, not the stored value of 0.3
== tests exact equality of the stored values, so it returns False
Correct method: test abs(a − b) < tol (or math.isclose) with a tolerance suited to the problem
questions.modelAnswer: Python floats are double-precision binary numbers. Decimals such as 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have infinite binary expansions, so each is stored as the nearest representable value. The rounding errors do not cancel: the computed sum is 0.30000000000000004, which differs from the stored value of 0.3, and == compares the stored values exactly, so the result is False. In numerical work you should instead test whether the numbers are close, for example abs(a − b) < 1e-12 or math.isclose(a, b), choosing the tolerance (absolute or relative) to suit the size of the numbers and the accuracy of the method.

questions.q:
What does the second line of output show?

def f(x, L=[]):
    L.append(x)
    return L

print(f(1))
print(f(2))
questions.why: The default list is created once, when f is defined, and the same list is reused, so after the second call it holds 1 and then 2 and [1, 2] is printed. [2] assumes a fresh empty list is made on every call, which is the misconception the example is designed to expose. [2, 1] assumes append adds to the front, but it adds to the end. None would be printed only if f had no return statement; here it returns L.

questions.q:
What does this code print?

x = 5
def h():
    x = 10
    return x
print(h(), x)
questions.why: The assignment inside h creates a local x, so h() returns 10 while the global x stays 5, giving '10 5'. '10 10' assumes the assignment inside the function changes the global variable, which needs a global statement. '5 5' assumes the function reads the global x, but the local assignment comes first. An UnboundLocalError arises only when a local name is read before it is assigned, which does not happen here.

questions.q: With A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) and B = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]), what is A * B?

With h = π/4 the values of sin x at 0, π/4, π/2, 3π/4, π are 0, √2/2, 1, √2/2, 0.
(a) Trapezium: (π/4)[½(0) + √2/2 + 1 + √2/2 + ½(0)] = (π/4)(1 + √2) ≈ 1.8961.
(b) Simpson: (π/12)[0 + 4(√2/2) + 2(1) + 4(√2/2) + 0] = (π/12)(4√2 + 2) ≈ 2.0046.
The exact value is [−cos x]₀^π = 2. The trapezium rule underestimates by about 0.104 (sin x is concave on [0, π], so the chords lie below the curve); Simpson's rule is out by only about 0.0046, reflecting its higher order of accuracy (O(h⁴) rather than O(h²)).

questions.q: What are the polar coordinates (r, θ), with 0 ≤ θ < 2π, of the point (−1, −√3)?
questions.why: r = √(1 + 3) = 2 and the point is in the third quadrant, so θ = π + π/3 = 4π/3. θ = π/3 is arctan(y/x) = arctan(√3) without the quadrant correction, which describes (1, √3). r = 4 forgets the square root in r = √(x² + y²). θ = 7π/6 comes from swapping x and y, using arctan(x/y) = π/6 and then adding π.

questions.q: In spherical coordinates (r, θ, φ) with θ measured from the positive z-axis, what is the volume element dV?
options: r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
r sin θ dr dθ dφ
questions.why: The small box has edges dr, r dθ and r sin θ dφ, so dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ. r² dr dθ dφ forgets that circles of constant θ have radius r sin θ, so the φ-edge is r sin θ dφ, not r dφ. r sin θ dr dθ dφ drops the factor r from the θ-edge r dθ. dr dθ dφ omits the Jacobian altogether.

questions.q: Show that the polar curve r = 4 sin θ is a circle, giving its centre and radius, and state the Cartesian coordinates of the point on it with θ = π/6.
markScheme: Multiply by r: r² = 4r sin θ
Substitute r² = x² + y², r sin θ = y: x² + y² = 4y
Complete the square: x² + (y − 2)² = 4, circle centre (0, 2), radius 2
θ = π/6: r = 2, point (2 cos π/6, 2 sin π/6) = (√3, 1)
questions.modelAnswer: Multiplying by r gives r² = 4r sin θ, i.e. x² + y² = 4y. Completing the square, x² + (y − 2)² = 4, which is the circle with centre (0, 2) and radius 2 (it passes through the origin). At θ = π/6, r = 4 × ½ = 2, so the point is (2 cos π/6, 2 sin π/6) = (√3, 1). Check: 3 + (1 − 2)² = 4.

questions.q: For f(x, y) = x² + 3xy, what is the directional derivative at (1, 2) in the direction of the vector (3, 4)?
questions.why: ∇f = (2x + 3y, 3x) = (8, 3) at (1, 2) and the unit vector is (3/5, 4/5), so the directional derivative is (24 + 12)/5 = 7.2. 36 is ∇f · (3, 4) without normalising the direction. √73 is |∇f|, the maximum rate of increase, which is in the direction of ∇f, not (3, 4). 3.6 comes from taking f_x = 2x and forgetting the 3y term, so ∇f is wrongly (2, 3).

questions.q: Let f(x, y) = xy/(x² + y²) for (x, y) ≠ (0, 0) and f(0, 0) = 0. Which statement is true?
options: f is differentiable at the origin because both partial derivatives exist there
f is continuous at the origin because f(x, 0) and f(0, y) both tend to 0
Both partial derivatives exist at the origin, but f is not continuous there
f_x(0, 0) does not exist because the formula has a zero denominator at the origin
questions.why: f(h, 0) = 0 and f(0, k) = 0, so both partial derivatives at the origin are 0, but along y = x the function equals ½, so it is not continuous at (0, 0). Claiming differentiability from the existence of partials is the classic error: differentiability needs more (for example, continuous partials). Checking only the two axes cannot prove continuity, as the line y = x shows. f_x(0, 0) must be found from the limit definition using f(0, 0) = 0, not from the formula, and that limit exists.

questions.q: Let z = f(x, y) where x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, and f has continuous first partial derivatives. Show that ∂z/∂θ = −y ∂f/∂x + x ∂f/∂y, and verify this for f(x, y) = x²y at r = 1, θ = π/4.
markScheme: Chain rule: ∂z/∂θ = f_x ∂x/∂θ + f_y ∂y/∂θ
∂x/∂θ = −r sin θ = −y and ∂y/∂θ = r cos θ = x, giving the result
For f = x²y: f_x = 2xy, f_y = x²; −y(2xy) + x(x²) = x³ − 2xy²
At x = y = √2/2: x³ − 2xy² = √2/4 − √2/2 = −√2/4; direct: z = cos²θ sin θ, dz/dθ = −2cos θ sin²θ + cos³θ = −√2/4 at π/4
questions.modelAnswer:
By the chain rule, ∂z/∂θ = f_x ∂x/∂θ + f_y ∂y/∂θ = f_x(−r sin θ) + f_y(r cos θ) = −y f_x + x f_y.
For f = x²y, f_x = 2xy and f_y = x², so ∂z/∂θ = −2xy² + x³. At r = 1, θ = π/4 we have x = y = √2/2, giving (√2/2)³ − 2(√2/2)³ = −(√2/2)³ = −√2/4 ≈ −0.354.
Directly, z = cos²θ sin θ, so dz/dθ = −2 cos θ sin²θ + cos³θ, which at θ = π/4 is −2(√2/2)³ + (√2/2)³ = −√2/4. The two agree.

questions.q: For f(x, y) = x³ + y³ − 3xy, what kind of point is (1, 1)?
questions.why: At (1, 1), f_x = 3x² − 3y = 0 and f_y = 3y² − 3x = 0, and D = (6)(6) − (−3)² = 27 > 0 with f_xx = 6 > 0, so it is a local minimum. A local maximum would need f_xx < 0; reading positive f_xx as a maximum reverses the meaning of the curvature. A saddle needs D < 0; getting one here usually comes from using f_xy² − f_xx f_yy, the wrong sign of D. 'Not a critical point' comes from differentiating −3xy incorrectly (for example taking f_x = 3x², which is 3 at (1, 1)).

questions.q: What is the second-order Taylor polynomial of f(x, y) = eˣ cos y about (0, 0)?
questions.why: At the origin f = 1, f_x = 1, f_y = 0, f_xx = 1, f_xy = −eˣ sin y = 0 and f_yy = −1, so P₂ = 1 + x + ½x² − ½y². The version with +½y² has the wrong sign for f_yy (cos y ≈ 1 − ½y²). Adding xy assumes a non-zero mixed derivative, but f_xy vanishes at the origin. 1 + x + x² − y² forgets the factor ½ in front of the second-order terms.

questions.q: Find and classify the critical point(s) of f(x, y) = x² + xy + y² − 3x.
markScheme: f_x = 2x + y − 3, f_y = x + 2y
Solving gives the single critical point (2, −1)
f_xx > 0, so local minimum, f(2, −1) = −3 (in fact global, as f is a positive definite quadratic plus linear terms)
questions.modelAnswer:
f_x = 2x + y − 3 = 0 and f_y = x + 2y = 0. From the second, x = −2y; substituting, −4y + y = 3, so y = −1 and x = 2. The only critical point is (2, −1).
f_xx = 2, f_yy = 2, f_xy = 1, so D = 2 × 2 − 1² = 3 > 0, and f_xx = 2 > 0: a local minimum. Its value is 4 − 2 + 1 − 6 = −3. Because the quadratic part x² + xy + y² is positive definite, this is also the global minimum.

questions.q: What is the length of the helix r(t) = (3 cos t, 3 sin t, 4t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π?
questions.why: |r′(t)| = √(9 sin²t + 9 cos²t + 16) = 5, so the length is 5 × 2π = 10π. 6π is the circumference of the circle the helix projects onto, ignoring the vertical motion. 8π is the vertical rise alone (4 × 2π). 14π adds the speed contributions 3 + 4 instead of combining them as √(3² + 4²).

questions.q: C is a curve from A to B, f is a scalar field and F is a vector field. If C is traversed in the opposite direction (from B to A), which of the following changes sign?
options: Both ∫_C f ds and ∫_C F · dr
questions.why: Reversing the direction reverses dr, so ∫_C F · dr changes sign, but ds measures length and is always positive, so ∫_C f ds is unchanged. Choosing f ds only gets the two integrals the wrong way round. Choosing both assumes every line integral is orientation-dependent. Choosing neither confuses independence of parametrisation (which both have, for parametrisations with the same direction) with independence of direction.

questions.q: Find the length of the curve y = x^(3/2) from x = 0 to x = 4.
markScheme: Uses L = ∫ √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx

questions.q: Which iterated integral equals ∫₀¹ ∫_y¹ f(x, y) dx dy for every continuous f?
questions.why: The region is 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, y ≤ x ≤ 1, the triangle below the line y = x; for fixed x, y runs from 0 to x, giving ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ f dy dx. ∫₀¹ ∫_x¹ f dy dx just swaps the letters in the limits and describes the other triangle, above y = x. ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ f dy dx integrates over the whole square. ∫₀¹ ∫₀^y f dy dx is not a valid iterated integral, because the inner limit depends on the variable being integrated.

questions.q: What is ∬ (x² + y²) dA over the disc x² + y² ≤ 4?
questions.why: In polar coordinates the integral is ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀² r² · r dr dθ = 2π × 4 = 8π. 16π/3 omits the Jacobian r, integrating r² dr instead of r³ dr. 16π multiplies the area 4π by the largest value of the integrand, 4, as if x² + y² were constant on the disc. 4π lets θ run only from 0 to π, which covers half the disc.

questions.q: Let R be the square |x| + |y| ≤ 1. Using the substitution u = x + y, v = x − y, evaluate ∬_R (x + y)² dA.
markScheme: Inverse: x = (u + v)/2, y = (u − v)/2
Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (½)(−½) − (½)(½) = −½; use absolute value ½
Region becomes the square −1 ≤ u ≤ 1, −1 ≤ v ≤ 1
Integral = ½ ∫₋₁¹ ∫₋₁¹ u² du dv = ½ × (2/3) × 2
Answer 2/3
questions.modelAnswer: Solving, x = (u + v)/2 and y = (u − v)/2, so ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = x_u y_v − x_v y_u = (½)(−½) − (½)(½) = −½, with absolute value ½. The four edges x + y = ±1 and x − y = ±1 become u = ±1 and v = ±1, so R corresponds to the square −1 ≤ u, v ≤ 1. Hence ∬_R (x + y)² dA = ∫₋₁¹ ∫₋₁¹ u² × ½ du dv = ½ × (2/3) × 2 = 2/3.

questions.q: For F = (x², yz, xz), what is div F at the point (1, 2, 3)?
questions.why: div F = ∂(x²)/∂x + ∂(yz)/∂y + ∂(xz)/∂z = 2x + z + x = 3x + z, which is 6 at (1, 2, 3). (2, 3, 1) lists the three partial derivatives without adding them, but divergence is a scalar. (−2, −3, 0) is the curl of F at that point, not the divergence. 8 comes from differentiating the third component xz with respect to x (giving z = 3) instead of with respect to z (giving x = 1).

questions.q: F = (2xy, x² + 3y²). What is ∫_C F · dr along any path C from (0, 0) to (1, 2)?
questions.why: P_y = 2x = Q_x, so F is conservative with potential φ = x²y + y³, and the integral is φ(1, 2) − φ(0, 0) = 2 + 8 = 10. 2 keeps only the x²y part of φ, forgetting the function g(y) = y³ that comes from the 3y² term. 8 keeps only the y³ part. 0 confuses path independence with the zero integral that holds only around closed curves.

questions.q: Show that F = (y cos(xy), x cos(xy) + 2y) is conservative on ℝ², find a potential φ, and evaluate ∫_C F · dr along any curve C from (0, 0) to (π/2, 1).
markScheme: P_y = cos(xy) − xy sin(xy) and Q_x = cos(xy) − xy sin(xy), equal
Domain ℝ² is simply connected and P, Q have continuous partials, so F is conservative
Integrating P in x: φ = sin(xy) + g(y); φ_y = x cos(xy) + g′(y) gives g = y²
φ = sin(xy) + y² (plus a constant)
questions.modelAnswer:
P = y cos(xy) gives P_y = cos(xy) − xy sin(xy), and Q = x cos(xy) + 2y gives Q_x = cos(xy) − xy sin(xy). These are equal, P and Q have continuous partial derivatives, and ℝ² is simply connected, so F is conservative.
Integrating P with respect to x gives φ = sin(xy) + g(y). Then φ_y = x cos(xy) + g′(y), which must equal x cos(xy) + 2y, so g(y) = y² and φ = sin(xy) + y².
By the fundamental theorem for line integrals, ∫_C F · dr = φ(π/2, 1) − φ(0, 0) = sin(π/2) + 1 − 0 = 2, for any path.

questions.q: Using Green's theorem, what is ∮_C (x² − y) dx + (x + y²) dy, where C is the boundary of the unit square [0, 1] × [0, 1] traversed anticlockwise?
questions.why: Q_x − P_y = 1 − (−1) = 2, so the integral is 2 × (area 1) = 2. 0 comes from a sign slip giving P_y = +1, so that Q_x − P_y appears to vanish. −2 is the clockwise value, or the result of computing P_y − Q_x. 1 uses only Q_x and forgets to subtract P_y.

questions.q: What is the outward flux of F = (x, y, z) through the sphere x² + y² + z² = 4?
questions.why: On a sphere of radius 2 the outward unit normal is (x, y, z)/2, so F · n = 2 everywhere and the flux is 2 × (surface area 16π) = 32π. 16π is the surface area alone, which forgets to multiply by F · n. 32π/3 is the volume of the ball, which is a different quantity. 0 assumes contributions cancel by symmetry, but F points outwards everywhere on the sphere, so every piece contributes positively.

questions.q: Use Green's theorem to show that the area enclosed by a positively oriented simple closed curve C is ½∮_C (x dy − y dx), and use this to find the area of the ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π.
markScheme: Take P = −y/2, Q = x/2, so Q_x − P_y = ½ + ½ = 1
Green: ½∮(x dy − y dx) = ∬_D 1 dA = area
dx = −a sin t dt, dy = b cos t dt; x dy − y dx = ab(cos²t + sin²t) dt = ab dt
Area = ½ ∫₀^(2π) ab dt = πab
questions.modelAnswer:
With P = −y/2 and Q = x/2 (continuous partial derivatives everywhere), Q_x − P_y = ½ − (−½) = 1. Green's theorem gives ∮_C P dx + Q dy = ½∮_C (x dy − y dx) = ∬_D 1 dA, which is the area of D.
For the ellipse, dx = −a sin t dt and dy = b cos t dt, so x dy − y dx = (ab cos²t + ab sin²t) dt = ab dt. Hence the area is ½ ∫₀^(2π) ab dt = πab.

questions.q:
Let f(x, y) = x³ + y³ − 3xy.
(a) Find all the critical points of f and classify each one. [8]
(b) Write down the second-order Taylor polynomial of f about (1, 1). [4]
(c) Find the rate of change of f at (2, 1) in the direction of the vector (1, 1), and state the direction and magnitude of the greatest rate of increase at that point. [4]
(d) Evaluate ∬_R f dA where R is the square [0, 1] × [0, 1]. [4]
markScheme: (a) f_x = 3x² − 3y, f_y = 3y² − 3x; solving gives y = x², x⁴ = x, so critical points (0, 0) and (1, 1)
(a) f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 6y, f_xy = −3; D = 36xy − 9
(a) (0, 0): D = −9 < 0, saddle; (1, 1): D = 27 > 0, f_xx = 6 > 0, local minimum, f = −1
(c) Greatest increase in direction (3, −1)/√10 with rate |∇f| = √90 = 3√10 ≈ 9.49
(d) ∫₀¹∫₀¹ (x³ + y³ − 3xy) dx dy = ¼ + ¼ − 3 × ½ × ½ = −¼
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) f_x = 3x² − 3y and f_y = 3y² − 3x. Setting both to zero gives y = x² and x = y², so x = x⁴, i.e. x(x³ − 1) = 0, giving x = 0 or x = 1 (the only real roots). The critical points are (0, 0) and (1, 1).
Second derivatives: f_xx = 6x, f_yy = 6y, f_xy = −3, so D = 36xy − 9 (f is a polynomial, so the second partials are continuous and the test applies).
At (0, 0): D = −9 < 0, so it is a saddle point (f = 0).
At (1, 1): D = 36 − 9 = 27 > 0 and f_xx = 6 > 0, so it is a local minimum, with f(1, 1) = 1 + 1 − 3 = −1.

(b) At (1, 1): f = −1, f_x = f_y = 0 (a critical point), f_xx = 6, f_yy = 6, f_xy = −3. With h = x − 1 and k = y − 1, P₂ = −1 + ½(6h² + 2(−3)hk + 6k²) = −1 + 3h² − 3hk + 3k². (Check at (1.1, 0.95): P₂ = −0.9475, f = −0.9466.)

(c) ∇f(2, 1) = (3 × 4 − 3 × 1, 3 × 1 − 3 × 2) = (9, −3). The unit vector in the direction (1, 1) is (1, 1)/√2, so the rate of change is (9 − 3)/√2 = 6/√2 = 3√2 ≈ 4.243. The greatest rate of increase is in the direction of ∇f, i.e. (3, −1)/√10, with magnitude |∇f| = √(81 + 9) = √90 = 3√10 ≈ 9.487.

(d) By Fubini's theorem (f is continuous on the rectangle), ∬_R f dA = ∫₀¹∫₀¹ x³ dx dy + ∫₀¹∫₀¹ y³ dx dy − 3∫₀¹ x dx ∫₀¹ y dy = ¼ + ¼ − 3 × ½ × ½ = ½ − ¾ = −¼.

questions.q:
Let F(x, y) = (2xy − y, x²).
(a) Show that F is not conservative. [3]
(b) Evaluate ∮_C F · dr directly, where C is the circle x² + y² = 4 traversed once anticlockwise. [6]
(c) Verify your answer to (b) using Green's theorem. [3]
(d) Evaluate ∫ F · dr from (0, 0) to (1, 1) (i) along the straight line y = x and (ii) along the parabola y = x². [6]
(e) Use Green's theorem to explain the difference between your two answers in (d). [2]
markScheme: (a) P_y = 2x − 1, Q_x = 2x; these differ (Q_x − P_y = 1 ≠ 0), so F is not conservative
(b) r = (2 cos t, 2 sin t); F · r′ = 4 sin²t − 16 cos t sin²t + 8 cos³t
(b) Integral over [0, 2π]: 4π + 0 + 0 = 4π
(c) ∬ (Q_x − P_y) dA = ∬ 1 dA = area of disc = 4π; hypotheses hold (polynomials, simple closed curve)
(d)(i) ∫₀¹ [(2t² − t) + t²] dt = ∫₀¹ (3t² − t) dt = ½
(d)(ii) ∫₀¹ [(2t³ − t²) + t² × 2t] dt = ∫₀¹ (4t³ − t²) dt = 1 − ⅓ = ⅔

(e) Out along the parabola and back along the line is an anticlockwise loop enclosing the region between y = x² and y = x (area 1/6); Green gives loop integral = 1/6 = ⅔ − ½, nonzero because F is not conservative
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) P = 2xy − y gives P_y = 2x − 1; Q = x² gives Q_x = 2x. Since Q_x − P_y = 1 ≠ 0, F is not conservative (a conservative C¹ field must have P_y = Q_x).

(b) Parametrise C by r(t) = (2 cos t, 2 sin t), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, so r′(t) = (−2 sin t, 2 cos t). Then P = 8 cos t sin t − 2 sin t and Q = 4 cos²t, so
F · r′ = (8 cos t sin t − 2 sin t)(−2 sin t) + 4 cos²t (2 cos t) = 4 sin²t − 16 cos t sin²t + 8 cos³t.
Over a full period, ∫ 4 sin²t dt = 4π, ∫ cos t sin²t dt = [sin³t/3] = 0 and ∫ cos³t dt = 0. So ∮_C F · dr = 4π.

(c) P and Q are polynomials, so they have continuous partial derivatives everywhere, and C is a positively oriented simple closed curve. Green's theorem gives ∮_C F · dr = ∬_D (Q_x − P_y) dA = ∬_D 1 dA = area of the disc of radius 2 = 4π, agreeing with (b).

(d)(i) On y = x, take r = (t, t), r′ = (1, 1), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1: F · r′ = (2t² − t) + t² = 3t² − t, so the integral is 1 − ½ = ½.
(ii) On y = x², take r = (t, t²), r′ = (1, 2t): F · r′ = (2t³ − t²) + t²(2t) = 4t³ − t², so the integral is 1 − ⅓ = ⅔.

(e) Going out along the parabola and back along the line forms a closed curve, anticlockwise because the parabola lies below the line on (0, 1). It encloses the region between y = x² and y = x, of area ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/6. By Green's theorem the loop integral is ∬ 1 dA = 1/6, so (ii) − (i) = ⅔ − ½ = 1/6, as found. The answers differ because F is not conservative.
